label: k8s-requests-vs-usage
text: The cluster looks full. But the nodes are barely using any resources. 🤔How is that possible?Because Kubernetes schedules pods based on resource requests, not actual usage.Here’s what happens:→ Kubernetes checks how much CPU and memory each pod requests.→ If the requests don’t fit on a node, the scheduler won’t place the pod there.→ Even if the node has plenty of unused CPU and memory, the pod may still remain pending.This helps keep resources available when workloads need them.But there’s a catch.Oversized requests reserve capacity that applications may never use.With a few services, it might not be a big problem.Across hundreds of workloads, that unused capacity can become a serious cost.Want to check your cluster?Run: kubectl describe nodesLook at the Allocated resources section for CPU

text: #BREAKING: The average size of monitored wildlife populations has fallen by 73% since 1970. But the Living Planet Report tells us something else, too... Elephants are growing in number in parts of southern Africa. Tigers are coming back. More green turtles are hatching. Pressure on the Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna is easing. None of this happened by chance. It’s the result of sustained action by people who refused to look away. This is what hope looks like in action. And if we’re going to outpace nature loss, we need more of it — from governments, businesses, investors and all of us. Because what happens next is not yet written. Share this and let’s turn hope into action for #OurLivingPlanet.Footage credit: WWF & Open Planet… more

text: 🏷️ The real price of AI is still unknown and human labor might outcompete AI.AI can already do images, text, video and voice - almost anything a person used to do as a paid service. Many of us consume these services every day, sometimes without knowing the result is AI-generated.So what is the problem? Isn't the economy already reshaped? Not yet. A real reshaping would mean human labor gets cheaper, because AI does the same job for less.
